artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let G be an abelian group (for instance the integers, a cyclic group, or the additive group of a finite field). Given a finite subset S of G as input, the sumset recognition problem asks to decide whether there exists a subset A of G such that
    S = A + A := { a + a' : a, a' ∈ A }.

A brute-force algorithm runs in time exponential in |S|: using the observation that if S = A + A then for every a ∈ A one has 2a ∈ S, S − 2a = (A − a) + (A − a), and A − a ⊆ S − 2a, one can iterate over s ∈ S and check all 2^{|S|} subsets of S − s as candidates for A − a, comparing their sumset to S − s.

Problem: Design an algorithm that, given a finite subset S of an abelian group G, decides whether S is of the form A + A for some subset A ⊆ G, and that runs in time substantially better than the exponential brute-force above (e.g. polynomial in |S|), or show that no such efficient algorithm exists. The question is of interest already in the special cases where G is torsion-free, G is cyclic, or G is the additive group of a finite field.
artifact.status_search_result: A 2024 preprint by Abboud, Fischer, and Safier proves that sumset recognition is NP-complete (for integers and over finite fields), and rules out 2^{o(n^{1/4})}-time algorithms under the Exponential Time Hypothesis. This shows a polynomial-time algorithm is unlikely, but the precise complexity (e.g., closing the gap between 2^{Ω(n^{1/4})} lower bound and 2^{O(n)} upper bound) remains open.

status_evidence.title: Recognizing Sumsets is NP-Complete
status_evidence.snippet: Granville asked whether one can efficiently recognize sumsets. We prove that the problem is NP-complete, and rule out 2^{o(n^{1/4})}-time algorithms under ETH.
status_evidence.claim: The decision problem of recognizing whether a finite set is a sumset A+A is NP-complete; no sub-exponential algorithm exists under ETH.
